cards.explanation: The answer is God's light. Job remembers God's lamp shining above his head, and he says he walked through the darkness by His light (Job 29:3). I think that's a big part of what he misses, friends. No flashlight on earth competes with that.

The answer is the Almighty. Job says that back then the Almighty was still with him, and his children were around him (Job 29:5). Notice that little word "still," friends. I think Job is looking at the empty space where all of that used to be.

The answer is True. Job says "…my steps were bathed in cream and the rock poured out for me streams of oil!" (Job 29:6) That's a man walking through plenty, friends. I've only ever been bathed in cookie crumbs, and I'm not complaining.

The answer is that they step back. Job says the young men saw him and withdrew (Job 29:8). That's how they responded when he went out to the city gate and took his seat in the public square. They stepped back and made room for him, friends. In the same verse, the old men rose to their feet.
The answer is False. Job says the old men rose to their feet (Job 29:8). The young men withdrew and the old men stood up, friends. Between the two, the square was doing a lot of moving.

The answer is that he rescued the poor who cried out. Job says people called him blessed because he rescued the poor who cried out and the fatherless who had no helper (Job 29:11-12). Notice what he names there, friends. It's the people he rescued.
The answer is False. Job says the dying man blessed him, and he made the widow's heart sing for joy (Job 29:13). Those are the people he's remembering, friends. I think it's a tender thing to recall.

The answer is clothed. Job says, "I put on righteousness, and it clothed me; justice was my robe and my turban." (Job 29:14) I wear an apron and a tall chef's hat, friends, and he wore righteousness and justice. His outfit wins.
The answer is feet. Job says he served as eyes to the blind and as feet to the lame (Job 29:15). Those are his words for how he served them, friends. That's a man you want at your side.

The answer is a long life ending in his own nest. Job says, "I will die in my nest and multiply my days as the sand." (Job 29:18) He thought he'd have a long life and end it at home, friends. I think that's a picture of a man who felt settled.

The answer is True. Job says, "My roots will spread out to the waters, and the dew will rest nightly on my branches." (Job 29:19) That's a tree with water at its roots and dew every night, friends. I think he pictured a life that would keep growing.

The answer is rain. Job says, "They waited for me as for rain and drank in my words like spring showers." (Job 29:23) Waiting for rain is waiting for something you really need, friends. That's how much his words meant to them.

The answer is king. Job says, "So I dwelt as a king among his troops, as a comforter of the mourners." (Job 29:25) And look at how he finishes that line, friends. Right after the king comparison, he says he dwelt as a comforter of the mourners.

The answer is his sheep dogs. Job says he would have refused to put the fathers of these younger men with his sheep dogs (Job 30:1). Those are strong words, friends, and they show how far apart he sees them from himself. The text just gives us his words, so I'll let them stand.
The answer is True. Job says they abhor him and keep far from him, and they do not hesitate to spit in his face (Job 30:10). I think this one hurts, friends. It's a heavy part of what he's saying.

The answer is that God has unstrung it. Job says, "…God has unstrung my bow and afflicted me…" (Job 30:11) and that the men have cast off restraint around him. Earlier he spoke of his bow being renewed in his hand, friends, and now he describes it unstrung (Job 29:20). A bow without a string can't shoot.

The answer is his dignity. Job says terrors are turned loose against him, and they drive away his dignity as by the wind (Job 30:15). That's something you can't pack up and carry home, friends. He adds that his prosperity has passed like a cloud.
The answer is False. Job says, "Night pierces my bones, and my gnawing pains never rest." (Job 30:17) Night doesn't give him any relief, friends. This is a heavy part of the passage.

The answer is True. Job says, "He throws me into the mud, and I have become like dust and ashes." (Job 30:19) Notice the word "like," friends. He's describing how low he feels he's been put. I think that's a hard thing to say out loud.

The answer is that He doesn't answer. Job says to God, "I cry out to You for help, but You do not answer; when I stand up, You merely look at me." (Job 30:20) These are Job's words, spoken straight to God, friends. I think it's honest, and it's heavy.

The answer is that he wept for them. Job asks, "Have I not wept for those in trouble? Has my soul not grieved for the needy?" (Job 30:25) He's pointing back at how he treated people in need, friends. It matches what he said earlier, that he rescued the poor who cried out (Job 29:12).

The answer is help. Job says, "I stand up in the assembly and cry for help." (Job 30:28) Back then he was the one who rescued the poor who cried out (Job 29:12), friends. Now Job is the one crying out.
The answer is True. Job says, "My skin grows black and peels, and my bones burn with fever." (Job 30:30) He's describing what's happening to his body, friends. It's a heavy line, so I'll let it be.

The answer is mourning. Job says, "My harp is tuned to mourning and my flute to the sound of weeping." (Job 30:31) His harp and his flute are tuned to grief, friends. I think it's a sad note to end a speech on.
